title: Spirulina: what it is and what nutrients it contains

seo.title: Spirulina: what it is and what nutrients it contains
seo.meta_description: Spirulina is dried cyanobacterial biomass rich in protein and iron. See its nutrition per 100 g and per realistic 7 g serving, plus the B12 caveat.
seo.search_intent: Understand what spirulina is and what nutrients it actually provides

excerpt: Commercial spirulina is dried biomass from Limnospira/Arthrospira cyanobacteria, not a marine seaweed. USDA reference data provide about 57.5 g protein and 28.5 mg iron per 100 g, but a 7 g tablespoon-sized amount gives roughly 4 g protein and 2 mg iron. It is not a reliable vitamin B12 source.
content_html:
Spirulina is sold beside seaweed powders and often called “blue-green algae,” but biologically it is a cyanobacterium. Species now classified in Limnospira/Arthrospira are cultivated, harvested, and dried into powder or tablets.

The powder is genuinely nutrient-dense. The catch is that 100-gram nutrition numbers describe far more spirulina than most people eat.

What dried spirulina contains

The USDA Standard Reference entry provides about 290 calories, 57.5 g protein, 7.7 g fat, and 23.9 g carbohydrate per 100 g. It also lists 28.5 mg iron, 195 mg magnesium, 1,363 mg potassium, and 6.1 mg copper.

NutrientPer 100 gPer 7 g
Calories290~20
Protein57.5 g~4.0 g
Fat7.7 g~0.5 g
Iron28.5 mg~2.0 mg
Magnesium195 mg~14 mg

The serving column is the useful reality check. Spirulina adds nutrients, but a spoonful is not nutritionally equivalent to a full serving of beans, tofu, eggs, meat, or fish.

Protein is its standout feature

Reviews commonly place spirulina around 50–70% protein by dry weight. It contains all essential amino acids, although amino-acid proportions, digestibility, and total dose still determine protein quality in practice.

Seven grams of the USDA reference provide about 4 g protein; 3 g provide only about 1.7 g.

Iron is concentrated, but servings are small

The 28.5 mg/100 g figure is high, while a 7 g amount supplies roughly 2 mg. Spirulina iron is non-heme iron, so the amount present is not identical to the amount absorbed.

What about vitamin B12?

This is the important exception to the “nutrient-rich” story. Laboratory methods can detect B12-like corrinoids in spirulina, but chemical characterization has shown that inactive pseudovitamin B12 predominates. Spirulina therefore should not replace a reliable B12 supplement or fortified food for people who need one.

Product quality matters

Cyanobacterial products can be contaminated if cultivation and testing are poor. The FDA notes that blue-green-algae products can be exposed to microcystins from contaminating cyanobacteria and emphasizes manufacturing controls and testing.

That makes traceability and reputable quality control more meaningful than unusually vivid color or broad “detox” claims.

Bottom line

Spirulina is a concentrated dry food that can add several grams of protein and some iron in a small serving. Its nutrition is real, but interpreting it per spoonful—not per 100 g—is what keeps the claims in proportion.

faq.question: Is spirulina really an algae?
faq.answer: It is commonly called blue-green algae, but biologically it is a photosynthetic cyanobacterium.

faq.question: How much protein is in 7 g of spirulina?
faq.answer: About 4 g using the USDA reference value of 57.5 g protein per 100 g.

faq.question: How much iron is in a serving?
faq.answer: About 2 mg in 7 g using the USDA value of 28.5 mg/100 g.

faq.question: Can spirulina supply vitamin B12?
faq.answer: It is not a reliable source because much of its B12-like material is inactive pseudovitamin B12.
